We assessed cardiac lipid import and export using arteriovenous lipidomics in a prospective observational study of 59 fasting patients undergoing catheter ablation for atrial arrhythmias. Paired arterial and coronary sinus plasma samples underwent targeted lipidomics, detecting 1,464 lipid species across 20 classes; 851 species were analyzed. Paired comparisons used separate Benjamini-Hochberg corrections for classes and species. The heart showed net uptake of FFAs (-122.4 μmol/L; 95% confidence interval [CI], -146.0 to -98.8; q = 1.49 × 10⁻13) and nonsignificant triglyceride uptake. Lysophosphatidylcholine was released (+4.32 μmol/L; 95% CI, 2.45 to 6.19; q = 2.12 × 10⁻⁴); no other class met q < 0.05. Thirty-two species met q < 0.05. Release from other classes offset FFA and triglyceride uptake on average, yielding a positive aggregate acyl-chain-equivalent difference (+28.2 μmol acyl-chain equivalents/L), although the CI included both uptake and release (95% CI, -112.8 to 169.2; P = 0.690). This study characterizes distinct patterns of cardiac lipid exchange under fasting conditions and provides a basis for studies in heart failure and broader cardiometabolic disease. Further studies are warranted to identify the sources of released lipids and explore cardiac lipid handling in the fed state.
ids: title:insights into human cardiac lipid dynamics through comprehensive arteriovenous lipidomics

title: Impact of Trimetazidine on Echocardiographic Indices and Clinical Outcomes in Ischemic Cardiomyopathy: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials.
abstract: Ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) is a major cause of chronic heart failure with impaired left ventricular (LV) function. Trimetazidine, a metabolic modulator that shifts energy utilization from fatty acid oxidation to glucose oxidation, may improve cardiac function in ischemic myocardium. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate trimetazidine's effect in patients with ICM compared to standard therapy alone. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, ProQuest, SAGE, EBSCO Host, Wiley, Science Direct, and SpringerLink databases until November 2024. Clinical trials assessing trimetazidine versus standard therapy in ICM were included. Data were analyzed using a random-effects model to calculate mean differences (MD) and relative risk (RR), with heterogeneity evaluated using the I2 statistic. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Trimetazidine significantly improved left ventricular ejection fraction (MD 6.35%, 95% CI: 4.63-8.07; p<0.05), reduced LV end-systolic diameter (MD -4.51 mm, p<0.05), LV end-diastolic diameter (MD -3.13 mm, p<0.05), and LV end-systolic volume (MD -14.20 ml, p<0.05). Exercise capacity improved markedly with a mean increase of 83.64 meters in the 6-minute walking test (p<0.05). NYHA class also improved (MD -0.80, p<0.05). However, no significant differences were found in anginal episodes or nitrate consumption. Trimetazidine as an adjunct to standard therapy improves cardiac function and exercise capacity in ischemic cardiomyopathy patients. It may be considered in patients with persistent symptoms or exercise intolerance despite optimal medical therapy. Further large-scale trials are warranted to assess long-term outcomes such as mortality and hospitalization.
ids: title:impact of trimetazidine on echocardiographic indices and clinical outcomes in ischemic cardiomyopathy an updated meta analysis of clinical trials

title: Tissue-Specific Angiogenic Responses to Exercise: Mechanisms and Research Advances.
abstract: Exercise is a pivotal non-pharmacological intervention for enhancing overall health, with a key underlying mechanism being the induction of adaptive angiogenesis across multiple organ systems. This narrative review discusses recent advances in exercise-induced angiogenesis, with a particular focus on its tissue- and organ-specific manifestations and underlying molecular mechanisms. The available evidence indicates that exercise integrates diverse signals-including mechanical stress, metabolic shifts, and hypoxic or ischemic stress-to upregulate key angiogenic factors, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1) and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), and to activate conserved signaling pathways including hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt), and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), thereby driving angiogenesis. This process exhibits tissue specificity: in skeletal muscle, it primarily enhances oxygen transport and metabolic efficiency; in bone, it couples with osteogenesis to maintain structural integrity; in the brain, it supports neuroplasticity and cognitive function; in the heart, it improves myocardial perfusion via angiogenesis and collateral remodeling (arteriogenesis); and in adipose tissue, it ameliorates the metabolic microenvironment. Furthermore, the mode and intensity of exercise, along with individual differences (such as age and health status), significantly influence the magnitude of its angiogenic effects. Accordingly, this review highlights the proposed role of exercise-induced angiogenesis in a range of conditions-including cardiovascular disease, sarcopenia, osteoporosis, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic syndrome-and we treat these relationships as potential mechanisms that require further validation rather than established therapeutic pathways. In the future, research should aim to define optimal exercise parameters, elucidate deeper molecular mechanisms, and investigate the translational potential of these insights for personalized clinical interventions.
ids: title:tissue specific angiogenic responses to exercise mechanisms and research advances

title: Doxorubicin-induced Cardiotoxicity in Dogs: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Doxorubicin, an anthracycline widely used in both human and veterinary oncology, is highly effective against a variety of malignancies in dogs, including lymphomas, sarcomas and carcinomas. Despite its efficacy, doxorubicin exposure can be associated with cardiotoxicity, which may present acutely or chronically, potentially leading to severe cardiac arrhythmia and congestive heart failure. Mechanisms underlying cardiotoxicity are multifactorial, including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage via topoisomerase IIβ, inflammation and dysregulated cell death pathways such as apoptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis. In dogs, known risk factors include higher cumulative dose, breed predisposition to idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, and higher body weight. Cardiac biomarkers, electrocardiography, echocardiography and other advanced imaging techniques have been employed to detect cardiac changes that can be seen also in the absence of clinical signs. However, current evidence is predominantly derived from experimental and retrospective research, highlighting the need for large prospective clinical studies to strengthen recommendations for monitoring and prevention. A deeper understanding of doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity in dogs is needed to identify factors influencing individual susceptibility, clarify the progression from subclinical damage to clinical cardiac dysfunction, and guide future research. Emerging approaches, including advanced echocardiography, microRNAs, proteomic biomarkers and pharmacokinetic modelling, may help improve early detection and guide more individualised dosing to minimise toxicity.
ids: title:doxorubicin induced cardiotoxicity in dogs a narrative review

title: Targeting mitochondrial morphofunctional homeostasis and oxidative stress: Iristectorigenin A protects against cardiac remodeling via SIRT6/FOXO1 signaling.
abstract: Myocardial remodeling, an essential pathological development in cardiovascular disease, is largely determined by disruptions in redox homeostasis and mitochondrial bioenergetic function. Iristectorigenin A (ITG), a naturally occurring isoflavone, exhibits a variety of pharmacological effects, including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. While so many protective effects, its specific effect on cardiac remodeling has not been reported previously. In this study, we aims to investigate the role of ITG in pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling with a particular focus on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress. We revealed that ITG mitigated TAC-induced cardiac remodeling and improved cardiac function, with the 20 mg/kg dose showing optimal efficacy; further escalation to 40 mg/kg provided no additional benefit. ITG attenuated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and inhibited activation of fibroblasts in vitro. Additionally, ITG treatment effectively suppressed oxidative stress and inflammation in the hearts of TAC mice, while improving mitochondrial morphology and the integrity of inner membrane structure. Notably, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis indicated a direct interaction between SIRT6 and ITG with micromolar affinity. Besides, sustained TAC- or PE-stimulation impaired cardiac sirtuin 6 (SIRT6) protein levels, which were partially reversed by ITG. More importantly, silencing SIRT6 and SIRT6 knockdown separately inhibited the protective effects of ITG in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, ITG promotes SIRT6 levels by inhibiting its ubiquitination degradation. Furthermore, the cardioprotective effect of ITG was concomitant with SIRT6 upregulation, deacetylation and dephosphorylation of forkhead box protein O1 (FOXO1) and the subsequent increased transcription of antioxidant genes. Collectively, we firstly discover that ITG inhibits oxidative stress and safeguards mitochondrial morphofunctional homeostasis in response to pathological stress through activating SIRT6/FOXO1 axis, suggesting the therapeutic potential of ITG in the treatment of cardiac hypertrophy and remodeling, providing a promising avenue for future research and potential clinical application. Schematic illustration of ITG's potential protective mechanism against cardiac hypertrophy.
ids: title:targeting mitochondrial morphofunctional homeostasis and oxidative stress iristectorigenin a protects against cardiac remodeling via sirt6 foxo1 signaling

title: Mechanisms and Advances in the Treatment of Arrhythmias Associated With Pulmonary Hypertension.
abstract: Arrhythmias related to pulmonary hypertension (PH) are major complications of disease progression and are associated with a significantly increased risk of death. The pathophysiology of these arrhythmias involves complex, multifaceted mechanisms. Arrhythmic substrates include electrical remodeling (ion channel imbalance, gap junction protein connexin 43 (Cx43) dysfunction, and autonomic neuropathy), structural remodeling (right ventricular hypertrophy/fibrosis), metabolic disorders (mitochondrial dysfunction and the Warburg effect), and chronic inflammation. Clinically, PH-related atrial arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation (AF)/flutter (AFL), are the most common. Diagnosis often requires combining ambulatory electrocardiography and implantable cardiac monitoring to detect subclinical events. Current treatment methods include optimizing PH-targeted therapy (e.g., dual- or triple-targeted drug therapy, soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulators), antiarrhythmic drugs, and catheter ablation, as well as emerging therapies such as Cx43 modulators, gene therapy (targeting bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2)/switch-independent 3A (SIN3A)), and microRNA (miRNA)-based regulation. Future work should focus on elucidating underlying mechanisms, developing precise risk stratification models, and formulating targeted individualized intervention strategies.
ids: title:mechanisms and advances in the treatment of arrhythmias associated with pulmonary hypertension

title: Leginsulin alleviates pathological cardiac hypertrophy potentially by regulating the oxidative stress-mediated MAPK signaling pathway
abstract: Abstract Pathological cardiac hypertrophy(PCH) is a critical driver of heart failure and is associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and abnormal stress-responsive signaling. This study aimed to investigate the protective effects of leginsulin, a naturally occurring soybean-derived peptide, against PCH and to elucidate its underlying mechanisms.Isoproterenol-induced cardiac hypertrophy was established in mice, and angiotensin II (AngII)-stimulated H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes were used as complementary in vitro models. Cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling were evaluated following leginsulin treatment.Leginsulin markedly attenuated cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in mice, as indicated by reduced cardiac enlargement, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and collagen accumulation. In AngII-stimulated H9c2 and AC16 cardiomyocytes, leginsulin suppressed the expression of hypertrophic and fibrotic markers. Furthermore, Leginsulin reduced oxidative stress by decreasing reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde levels while enhancing superoxide dismutase activity. In parallel, leginsulin preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, increased adenosine triphosphate production, and improved mitochondrial network integrity. Mechanistically, leginsulin selectively suppressed AngII -induced activation of c-Jun N-terminal kinase and extracellular signal-regulated kinase signaling whereasp38 signaling was not significantly affected.Leginsulin protects against PCH and fibrosis by maintaining redox balance, preserving mitochondrial function, and regulating stress-responsive signaling pathways. These findings reveal a physiological role of leginsulin in cardiac stress adaptation and highlight its potential as a natural regulator of PCH.
ids: title:leginsulin alleviates pathological cardiac hypertrophy potentially by regulating the oxidative stress mediated mapk signaling pathway

title: LGR6 couples maresin 1 signaling to glycolytic flux and protein lactylation for the rescue of diabetic cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Background Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DbCM) is driven by metabolic inflexibility and impaired mitochondrial clearance. While the pro-resolving lipid mediator Maresin 1 (MaR1) shows therapeutic promise, its capacity to correct the underlying metabolic-epigenetic disturbances in DbCM remains undefined. Materials Db/db mice and palmitic acid (PA)-exposed H9c2 cardiomyocytes were treated with MaR1. Cardiac function and structure were assessed by echocardiography and histological analysis. Myocardial oxidative stress, inflammation, and key molecular pathways were evaluated via immunoblotting, qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and transmission electron microscopy. The role of the putative receptor LGR6 was investigated using siRNA-mediated knockdown. Results MaR1 improved cardiac diastolic function, attenuated pathological hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis, and reduced oxidative stress and inflammatory markers in db/db mice. Mechanistically, MaR1 activated AMPK signaling, restoring the expression of crucial enzymes for both fatty acid oxidation (CPT1B) and glycolysis (PFK-1, HK2). This metabolic reprogramming elevated intracellular lactate, which in turn replenished the deficient global protein lysine lactylation (Kla). Concurrently, MaR1 reactivated the PINK1/Parkin pathway, restoring mitophagy-associated signaling. In vitro, exogenous lactate supplementation recapitulated these effects. Importantly, LGR6 silencing abrogated all MaR1-induced benefits, including glycolytic activation, lactylation rescue, and mitophagic recovery. Conclusion MaR1 protects against DbCM by signaling through LGR6 to restore metabolic flexibility, thereby fueling a lactate-dependent lactylation program that is critically associated with the reactivation of mitochondrial quality control via mitophagy. This study unveils a critical metabolic-epigenetic axis as a novel therapeutic target.
ids: title:lgr6 couples maresin 1 signaling to glycolytic flux and protein lactylation for the rescue of diabetic cardiomyopathy

title: Analysis of myocardial work in different obesity phenotypes and its association with epicardial adipose tissue.
abstract: To evaluate subclinical cardiac dysfunction across distinct obesity phenotypes using myocardial work (MW) indices, and to investigate the moderating role of epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) on MW impairment. One hundred ninety-two participants were categorized by BMI and metabolic status into four groups: metabolically healthy normal weight (MHNW), metabolically healthy obesity (MHO), metabolically unhealthy normal weight (MUNW), and metabolically unhealthy obesity (MUO). MW indices were measured using speckle-tracking echocardiography. EAT volume was quantified from ECG-gated CT scans. Associations were analyzed using ANCOVA and regression models. Despite no significant differences in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) among the groups, MUNW and MUO individuals exhibited significantly impaired MW, characterized by lower global work index (GWI), global constructive work (GCW), and global work efficiency (GWE), alongside higher global waste work (GWW), compared with MHNW controls. MHO patients showed significantly better MW profiles than MUNW and MUO groups. EAT volume was increased in all obesity phenotype groups. Although no direct association was found between EAT volume and MW indices, EAT volume significantly moderated the relationship between Metabolically Unhealthy (MUH) and both GWE and GWW. MW detects subclinical dysfunction earlier than LVEF across obesity phenotypes, with impairment progressively worsening from MHO to MUNW to MUO. In metabolically unhealthy individuals with increased EAT volume, more pronounced reductions in GWE and elevations in GWW were observed. This study has been registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry under the registration number ChiCTR2500100754 (registration date: April 15, 2025).
ids: title:analysis of myocardial work in different obesity phenotypes and its association with epicardial adipose tissue

title: Bidirectional metabolic-vascular feedback loops in heart failure: From myocardial energetics to multisystem cardiometabolic crosstalk.
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a multisystem syndrome in which myocardial dysfunction is shaped by metabolic, vascular, and extracardiac abnormalities. Across HFrEF and HFpEF, impaired substrate utilization, mitochondrial function, endothelial signaling, coronary microvascular function, and mechano-energetic coupling disrupt the matching of ATP supply to cardiac demand, while obesity, insulin resistance, inflammation, and vascular stiffness further accentuate cardiometabolic HFpEF. In this Review, we integrate these processes into five self-reinforcing metabolic-vascular circuits: substrate-perfusion mismatch; mitochondrial reactive oxygen species-endothelial dysfunction; endothelial metabolism-nitric oxide-myocardial stiffness; immunometabolic-microvascular inflammation-fibrosis; and afterload-mechano-energetic uncoupling. We also examine how adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, liver, and kidney amplify these circuits. Together, this framework links myocardial energetic dysfunction with systemic vascular-metabolic stress and highlights circuit-directed opportunities for phenotype-informed HF therapy.
ids: title:bidirectional metabolic vascular feedback loops in heart failure from myocardial energetics to multisystem cardiometabolic crosstalk

title: Methyl indole-3-acetate mediates myricetin-induced brown adipose tissue activation and reproductive-metabolic improvement in PCOS mice.
abstract: In brief: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder with limited treatments. This study shows that the flavonoid myricetin increases the gut metabolite methyl indole-3-acetate, which activates brown fat to improve PCOS symptoms in mice. Abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is frequently associated with alterations in gut microbiota composition, although the specific microbial metabolites that influence ovarian function remain incompletely understood. Myricetin has been reported to improve reproductive and metabolic features in experimental PCOS models and to activate brown adipose tissue (BAT); however, whether these effects are mediated by the gut microbiota has not been clarified. In dehydroepiandrosterone-induced PCOS mice, myricetin treatment was associated with improved estrous cyclicity, ovarian morphology, fertility, and insulin sensitivity. These changes coincided with notable shifts in gut microbial composition and the serum metabolome. Integrated multiomics analysis suggested that methyl indole-3-acetate (MIA), a microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolite, was among the metabolites most consistently elevated following myricetin administration. Fecal microbiota transplantation from myricetin-treated donors partially improved ovarian function and glucose homeostasis in recipient mice. Supplementation with MIA enhanced BAT thermogenesis and the expression of thermogenic genes, whereas surgical removal of interscapular BAT attenuated the metabolic improvements observed with MIA. Together, these results suggest that myricetin may improve PCOS-like reproductive and metabolic disturbances through microbiota remodeling and elevated production of MIA, which supports BAT activity. This study identifies MIA as a previously unrecognized microbiota-derived metabolite that links gut microbial metabolism to BAT function and reproductive outcomes, providing new mechanistic insight into how dietary compounds may influence ovarian function in PCOS.
ids: 10.1093/reprod/xaag110
title:methyl indole 3 acetate mediates myricetin induced brown adipose tissue activation and reproductive metabolic improvement in pcos mice

title: ZBP1-medicated PANoptosis-related signaling contributes to PD-1 inhibitor-associated cardiotoxicity.
abstract: The growing use of PD-1 inhibitor has led to an increased incidence of immune-related cardiotoxicity, a condition associated with high mortality. Understanding its underlying mechanisms is critical for early detection and targeted treatment. This study integrated transcriptomic and single-cell transcriptomic data to identify potential pathways involved in immune-related cardiotoxicity. BMS-1- and anti-PD-1 antibody-induced mouse models were established for in vivo validation. In vitro, AC16 cardiomyocytes were co-cultured with Jurkat cells in the presence of the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab. Cardiac function, myocardial injury, cell death, inflammatory cytokines, PANoptosis-related signaling, mitochondrial function, and cytosolic mtDNA were assessed. Bioinformatic analyses identified activation of PANoptosis-related pathways and increased ZBP1 expression in immune-related cardiotoxicity. Pembrolizumab induced cardiomyocyte injury and increased IFN-γ and TNF-α production. Anti-PD-1 antibody treatment caused cardiac dysfunction and myocardial injury in mice, accompanied by increased ZBP1 and apoptosis-, pyroptosis-, and necroptosis-related markers. ZBP1 overexpression aggravated, whereas ZBP1 knockdown attenuated, cardiomyocyte injury and PANoptosis-related signaling. Cardiac ZBP1 knockdown also improved cardiac function and reduced myocardial injury in anti-PD-1-treated mice without suppressing inflammatory cytokine levels. Furthermore, PD-1 inhibitor induced mitochondrial dysfunction, altered mitochondrial dynamics, and increased cytosolic mtDNA accumulation, with enhanced ZBP1 association with Z-DNA-associated signals. ZBP1-mediated PANoptosis-related signaling may contribute to PD-1 inhibitor-associated cardiotoxicity, potentially linking inflammatory activation and mitochondrial/mtDNA stress to cardiomyocyte injury.
ids: title:zbp1 medicated panoptosis related signaling contributes to pd 1 inhibitor associated cardiotoxicity

title: Astragaloside IV and Ferroptosis Modulation in Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy: Current Evidence, an Integrative Hypothesis, and Future Directions.
abstract: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is initially an adaptive response to sustained mechanical, neurohormonal, or metabolic stress; however, it can progress to fibrosis, contractile dysfunction, arrhythmia, and heart failure. Ferroptosis is a type of regulated cell death caused by iron-dependent phospholipid peroxidation. Evidence consistent with ferroptosis, such as disrupted iron homeostasis, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired antioxidant defense, has been reported in experimental models of pathological cardiac hypertrophy; however, these findings do not by themselves establish ferroptosis as a cause of hypertrophic remodeling. Astragaloside IV (AS-IV) is a cycloartane-type triterpene saponin from Astragalus species that has shown anti-hypertrophic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, metabolic-regulatory and mitochondrial-protective effects in experimental cardiovascular models. AS-IV has also shown anti-ferroptotic effects in several cardiac and extra-cardiac disease models by means of Nrf2-centred antioxidant defense, regulation of SLC7A11/GPX4, p53 signaling, CD36-dependent lipid handling, and 14-3-3η-linked regulation of GPX4 stability. Nevertheless, whether ferroptosis inhibition directly contributes to the anti-hypertrophic effect of AS-IV in pathological cardiac hypertrophy remains unproven because direct causal validation in dedicated hypertrophy models is lacking. This review collects evidence on the biology of ferroptosis in pathological cardiac hypertrophy, the established anti-hypertrophic pharmacology of AS-IV, its reported anti-ferroptotic effects, and relevant pharmacokinetic considerations. Based on this, we propose that AS-IV may reduce the susceptibility of cardiomyocytes to ferroptosis and thus partially inhibit pathological cardiac remodeling; however, this is not yet a proven mechanism. Direct verification requires etiologically distinct hypertrophy models, multi-modal ferroptosis measurements, targeted genetic or pharmacological disruption, dose-response and pharmacokinetic experiments, and cell-type-resolved analysis.
ids: title:astragaloside iv and ferroptosis modulation in pathological cardiac hypertrophy current evidence an integrative hypothesis and future directions

title: The cardiac calcium handling machinery is remodeled in Friedreich ataxia.
abstract: Background Friedreich ataxia (FA) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of the GAA triplet repeat in the frataxin (FXN) gene, leading to reduced FXN expression. FA commonly affects the heart, causing hypertrophy, heart failure, and fibrosis. The mechanisms of FA-associated cardiac dysfunction may involve disrupted calcium (Ca 2+ ) handling and mitochondrial impairment. Objective This study aimed to investigate whether abnormalities in Ca 2+ handling machinery contributes to cardiac dysfunction in FA. Methods Human left ventricular tissue from patients with FA and unaffected donors, and an FXN knock-out (FXN-KO) mouse model, were analyzed. In mice, cardiac function was assessed by echocardiography and electrocardiography. The expression of Ca 2+ -handling proteins was evaluated with Western blotting, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction, and immunofluorescence. Single-cell contractility and Ca 2+ transients were measured in isolated ventricular myocytes. Mitochondrial function was assessed via confocal imaging to quantify mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψ m ) and reactive oxygen species. Results FXN-KO mice exhibited significant reductions in ejection fraction, stroke volume, fractional shortening, and cardiac output, with increased left ventricular mass and elevated end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes. Strain analysis revealed increased global and peak longitudinal strain. On electrocardiogram, the RR, PR, QRS, and QTc intervals were prolonged. Both human FA and FXN-KO hearts showed downregulation of sarco or endoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ -ATPase 2a and ryanodine receptor 2, with reduced phospholamban phosphorylation. FXN-KO mice also showed upregulation of mitochondrial Ca 2+ -handling proteins, including mitochondrial Ca 2+ uniporter and voltage-dependent anion channel, depolarized Δψ m , and elevated reactive oxygen species. Conclusion Cardiac dysfunction in FA is associated with impaired Ca 2+ handling, mitochondrial dysregulation, and systolic impairment, identifying potential molecular targets for therapy.
ids: title:the cardiac calcium handling machinery is remodeled in friedreich ataxia
title:the cardiac calcium handling machinery is remodeled in friedreich s ataxia

title: Fatty Heart in T2DM- A New Proposal in The Cardio Reno Metabolic Syndrome Continuum
abstract: Background: and Objectives: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) represents a major public health issue due to its prevalence and strong association with cardiovascular disease (CVD). Emerging evidence highlights Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) as an active endocrine organ implicated in metabolic regulation, inflammation and thermogenesis. This article aims to scope the available evidence related to EAT´s role in the development and management of CVD in adults with T2DM. Materials and Methods: This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in Pubmed, Scopus and Cochrane using the terms “Epicardial Fat”, “Diabetes Mellitus” and “Cardiovascular Disease”. Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical trials, and observational studies were included and screened. Articles with exclusively animal experiments, non-extractable data and no relevance with the research question were excluded. Results: 39 studies were included. Evidence showed that increased EAT thickness is associated with higher risk of coronary artery disease, ischemia, heart failure, and repolarization disorders. Interventions with SGLT2i and GLP1-RA reduced EAT’s volume and inflammatory profile. Data on dual GLP1/GIP agonists remains limited. Conclusions: Current evidence supports EAT as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target in cardiovascular management of T2DM patients. Even so, available clinical trials are limited, highlighting the need of more robust studies to establish its clinical value.
ids: title:fatty heart in t2dm a new proposal in the cardio reno metabolic syndrome continuum

title: Coronary microvascular dysfunction in HFpEF: pathophysiologic mechanisms, diagnosis, treatments, and the amplifying potential of sepsis.
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a heterogeneous syndrome in which coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) emerges as a central, prevalent pathobiologic substrate across multiple phenotypic clusters. CMD in HFpEF arises from intertwined mechanisms including systemic inflammation, impaired NO-cGMP-PKG signaling, microvascular rarefaction and fibrosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and ventriculoarterial decoupling that together promote subendocardial ischemia, diastolic stiffness, reduced reserve, and adverse outcomes. Advances in diagnostics, both invasive and non-invasive, as well as individualized medical and surgical intervention, create avenues of opportunity to prevent CMD-mediated HFpEF at a precise level. Sepsis and septic shock can superimpose an acute second hit on this chronically injured microvasculature, precipitating acute decompensation and potentially accelerating long-term CMD-driven remodeling in vulnerable HFpEF patients. While mechanistically plausible, this association remains hypothesis-generating. Advanced hemodynamics and diagnostics with tailored vasopressor and inotropic management need to be better studied in complex states of septic shock in HFpEF patients to understand the influence of CMD in such states.
ids: title:coronary microvascular dysfunction in hfpef pathophysiologic mechanisms diagnosis treatments and the amplifying potential of sepsis

title: Metabolic stress exacerbates Ca<sup>2+</sup> dysregulation and arrhythmias in catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
abstract: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is a genetic arrhythmic syndrome caused by mutations in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) calcium (Ca 2+ ) release channel RyR2 or its accessory proteins, including calsequestrin-2 (CASQ2). RyR2 dysfunction or leak is the hallmark feature of CPVT and directly triggers arrhythmias. Despite this electrical instability, CPVT hearts are typically anatomically normal and lack pathological remodelling. Therefore, we hypothesized that introducing additional stressors, such as metabolic stress, would worsen cardiac arrhythmias and potentially trigger pathological remodelling. To test this hypothesis, metabolic stress was introduced by crossbreeding a CPVT model of CASQ2 -/- mice with the Akita mouse, a genetic model of diabetes that also lacks cardiac remodelling. We found that dysregulation of myocyte Ca 2+ handling was exacerbated in Akita-CASQ2 -/- cells, which exhibited slower Ca 2+ transient decay kinetics and increased arrhythmogenic Ca 2+ waves. Akita-CASQ2 -/- mice also displayed more severe arrhythmias, diastolic dysfunction, and cardiac hypertrophy, but without evidence of fibrosis, cell death, or worsened metabolic dysfunction. Finally, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production was increased in Akita-CASQ2 -/- cardiomyocytes, which may contribute to the more severe pathological phenotype. Overall, our results suggest that metabolic stress can aggravate dysregulated myocyte Ca 2+ handling and promote cardiac dysfunction in CPVT hearts.
ids: title:metabolic stress exacerbates ca sup 2 sup dysregulation and arrhythmias in catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia

title: Disulfidptosis in heart failure: an emerging mechanism awaiting exploration.
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a major cardiovascular syndrome with increasing global incidence and mortality rates. Cardiomyocyte injury and ventricular remodeling are central pathological processes driving HF progression. Although several forms of regulated cell death have been implicated in HF, the mechanisms underlying cardiomyocyte injury remain poorly understood. Disulfidptosis, proposed in 2023, is a metabolism-related form of regulated cell death triggered by the depletion of the cellular reducing capacity. Evidence from tumor cell models indicates that under glucose-restricted conditions, cells with high SLC7A11 expression may exhibit insufficient NADPH production due to impaired pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) activity, resulting in disulfide stress, aberrant disulfide cross-linking of filamentous actin (F-actin), cytoskeletal collapse, and cell death. During HF progression, cardiomyocytes commonly undergo glucose metabolic remodeling, redox imbalance, and cytoskeletal abnormalities, which may create a permissive context for disulfidptosis-like injuries. However, direct experimental evidence demonstrating disulfidptosis in cardiomyocytes or the failing myocardium remains limited. Rather than treating transcriptomic associations as evidence of a defined cell-death programme, this review integrates HF-associated metabolic remodelling, impaired redox buffering, and cytoskeletal vulnerability within a testable mechanistic framework. It further defines a staged validation strategy for determining whether disulfidptosis occurs in cardiomyocytes or other myocardial cell populations.
ids: title:disulfidptosis in heart failure an emerging mechanism awaiting exploration

title: Loss of myosin VI leads to age-dependent changes in the maintenance of heart ventricle mitochondria
abstract: Aims We have recently shown that unconventional myosin VI (MVI), a unique actin-based molecular motor, is involved in age-progressive cardiac dysfunction. Here, we aimed at elucidation of mechanisms of MVI involvement in this phenotype. We propose that MVI plays a role as a regulator of mitochondria quality control as well as of their organization and distribution in the heart, an organ with extremely high energy demand. Methods and results We analyzed heart samples from MVI knockout mice (Snell’s waltzer) and their heterozygous littermates: newborns (P0), 3-month-old (3m), and 12-month-old (12m) mice. Transmission electron microscopy and immunostaining revealed that loss of MVI affected mitochondria network organization and promoted mitochondria clustering in the perinuclear space. Moreover, accumulation of large functional mitochondria, increase in total mitochondria mass with a concomitant increase in the amount of damaged mitochondria were observed in 12m hearts. The Western blot technique revealed that loss of MVI, at all examined time points, did not affect the activity of AMPK, the key energy balance sensor, and the level of the respiratory chain components. However, in P0 samples it affected the levels of OPA1, involved in mitochondria fusion, and the activity of S6, the downstream effector of mTOR. Also, loss of MVI affected autophagy/mitophagy activity in P0 hearts, leading to accumulation of autophagosomes. A pull-down assay enabled identification of over three hundred potential MVI-binding partners; among them were proteins involved in mitochondria organization and functions, autophagy, ion transport, and cell respiration. Conclusion Taken together, our results indicate that loss of MVI evokes changes disclosed already in newborns that lead to profound alterations in the mitochondria organization and maintenance with age. We believe that accumulation of changes in mitochondria structure, distribution and quality commits to the age-progressing cardiac remodeling and dysfunction. Graphical Abstract
ids: title:loss of myosin vi leads to age dependent changes in the maintenance of heart ventricle mitochondria

title: Probiotics-derived postbiotics improve host metabolic syndrome by activating the adipocyte thermogenic signaling pathway in high-fat diet-fed mice.
abstract: Metabolic syndrome, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity, represents a global health challenge. While probiotics can modulate host metabolism, postbiotics (inanimate microbial preparations) have emerged as potentially safer and more stable therapeutic alternatives. The current study investigates the effects of postbiotics derived from five human-origin bacterial strains in mice model with high-fat diet-induced metabolic syndrome. Using multi-omics profiling, we demonstrate that supplementation of postbiotics significantly ameliorates weight gain, improves glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, and alleviates hepatic steatosis. Transcriptomic analysis indicates that the treatment upregulated adipocyte genes related to thermogenesis and fatty acid oxidation while downregulating hepatic lipid synthesis. Most importantly, the intervention reshapes the gut microbiota structure. Target metabolomics reveals that this microbial remodeling is accompanied by a significant elevation of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), a tryptophan-derived microbial metabolite, in the host serum. Functional studies in primary adipocytes confirm that IAA is sufficient to trigger thermogenic gene expression and activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) signaling. These findings suggest a mechanism where postbiotics improve metabolic health by modulating the gut ecosystem to enrich beneficial metabolites like IAA, which in turn ameliorates the metabolic syndrome and promotes adipocyte thermogenesis and lipolysis. The present research supports postbiotics as a promising therapeutic strategy for metabolic syndrome and highlights the importance of the gut microbiota-metabolite axis.
ids: title:probiotics derived postbiotics improve host metabolic syndrome by activating the adipocyte thermogenic signaling pathway in high fat diet fed mice

title: Ketogenic diet attenuates cardiac aging through inhibiting CD36/MAPK-mediated lipid accumulation: Comparable effects in aged male and female mice.
abstract: Aging is accompanied by a decline in circulating ketone bodies and progressive cardiac dysfunction, yet whether dietary ketone repletion counteracts cardiac aging in a sex-specific manner remains unclear. Here, we first investigated the associations between plasma ketone bodies and cardiac function in a human cohort, comprising 120 adults (44.78 ± 10.97 years; 66 male/54 female) and 121 aged individuals (69.59 ± 6.88 years; 75 male/46 female). And, we then evaluated the therapeutic potential of an 8-week ketogenic diet (KD) in physiologically aged mice (22 months, both sexes), which were daily supplemented with either chow diet (3.79 kcal/g, Aged group) or KD (7.24 kcal/g, Aged+KD group). In humans, circulating β-hydroxybutyrate (β-HB) levels were significantly lower in aged human individuals and positively correlated with key parameters of cardiac function, including ejection fraction (EF), fractional shortening (FS) and the ratio of early to late diastolic filling velocity (E/A ratio). In aged mice, 8-week KD supplementation elevated cardiac β-HB concentrations and attenuated cardiac remodeling in both sexes. Notably, KD improved systolic/diastolic function (e.g., EF, FS and E/A ratio), preserved mitochondrial function, reduced myocardial lipid accumulation, and ameliorated systemic dyslipidemia equivalently in both sexes. Mechanistically, KD suppressed CD36 membrane translocation and MAPK activation, whereas CD36 upregulation abolished these protective effects, establishing a causal role of the CD36/MAPK pathway in KD-mediated cardioprotection. Altogether, these findings identify β-HB as a biomarker of cardiac aging and show that KD rescues age-related cardiomyopathies through CD36-MAPK-mediated lipid metabolic regulation, with equivalent benefits in both sexes.
ids: title:ketogenic diet attenuates cardiac aging through inhibiting cd36 mapk mediated lipid accumulation comparable effects in aged male and female mice

title: Perivascular fat attenuation index improves the identification of functional myocardial ischemia beyond traditional risk factors: a coronary CT angiography-derived fractional flow reserve study.
abstract: Perivascular fat attenuation index (FAI) derived from coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is a novel imaging biomarker of coronary inflammation. However, its incremental value in predicting functional myocardial ischemia, defined by CT-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR), beyond traditional cardiovascular risk factors and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) volume remains unclear. A total of 380 consecutive patients who underwent clinically indicated CCTA with CT-FFR evaluation were retrospectively analyzed. Functional ischemia was defined as CT-FFR ≤0.80. Patients were stratified into low and high FAI groups based on the optimal cutoff value of -81.32 Hounsfield Units (HU). Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of ischemia. The incremental diagnostic performance of adding FAI to a baseline clinical model was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), continuous net reclassification improvement (NRI), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and decision curve analysis (DCA). Despite comparable baseline profiles for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, body mass index, and glycemic status (P > 0.05), patients in the high FAI group exhibited significantly lower CT-FFR values (0.75 ± 0.13 vs. 0.79 ± 0.12, P = 0.0017). After adjusting for age, gender, traditional cardiovascular risk factors, and EAT volume, average FAI remained a robust independent predictor of functional ischemia [Adjusted Odds Ratio [OR]: 1.056 per 1 HU increase; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 1.019-1.096; P = 0.004]. Notably, EAT volume did not reach statistical significance in the multivariate model (P = 0.584). The addition of FAI to the clinical model resulted in a modest, non-significant improvement in AUC (0.731 vs. 0.707, P = 0.087), but yielded significant improvement in risk reclassification (continuous NRI: 0.339, P = 0.001; IDI: 0.024, P = 0.002). Subgroup analysis demonstrated a consistent risk trend across varying degrees of stenosis, age, and body mass index categories (OR range: 1.03-1.07). DCA confirmed superior net clinical benefit for the FAI-integrated model across a wide threshold probability range (25%-75%). Coronary perivascular FAI is an independent imaging marker for CT-FFR-defined functional ischemia and provides incremental value beyond traditional risk factors and EAT volume. These findings support FAI as a non-invasive marker of coronary inflammation that may refine risk stratification for functionally significant coronary artery disease. However, as CT-FFR mainly reflects epicardial physiology, the association between FAI and microvascular dysfunction remains to be determined.
ids: title:perivascular fat attenuation index improves the identification of functional myocardial ischemia beyond traditional risk factors a coronary ct angiography derived fractional flow reserve study

title: Maternal protein restriction during lactation programs peripheral insulin sensitivity and reduces UCP1 abundance in interscapular brown adipose tissue of adult male Wistar rats.
journal: Journal of developmental origins of health and disease
abstract: Maternal protein restriction during lactation is associated with stunted growth and hyperphagia in adult offspring, yet its long-term effects on mitochondrial uncoupling-related proteins in interscapular brown adipose tissue (iBAT) remain unknown. This study investigated how postnatal protein undernutrition affects thermogenic regulators and metabolic programming in adult males. Dams received either a low-protein (LP; 4% protein) or normal-protein (NP; 20.5% protein) diet during the first two weeks of lactation. Thereafter, the NP diet was provided to LP dams until weaning and to all offspring from weaning to PND 90. Male offspring were euthanized at postnatal day 90 for somatic, biochemical, hormonal, and iBAT UCP1 and β3-AR protein analyses. Compared with NP controls, LP offspring exhibited reduced body mass, length, and visceral adiposity, despite increased food consumption (all p 0.05). These findings indicate that maternal protein undernutrition during lactation programmed a persistent metabolic phenotype characterized by hyperphagia, reduced somatic growth and visceral adiposity, increased peripheral insulin sensitivity, and lower iBAT UCP1 protein abundance. Collectively, these results suggest long-term alterations in energy partitioning and the iBAT molecular phenotype, although functional thermogenesis was not assessed.
ids: title:maternal protein restriction during lactation programs peripheral insulin sensitivity and reduces ucp1 abundance in interscapular brown adipose tissue of adult male wistar rats

title: Prospects for adiponectin-based therapeutics in myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury.
summary: Addressed myocardial ischemia‑reperfusion injury by reviewing strategies to boost adiponectin signaling, including peptide and small‑molecule mimetics, in animal models. Found that enhancing the adiponectin‑AdipoR axis consistently reduced infarct size, improved function, and lowered apoptosis, inflammation, and microvascular no‑reflow. This matters because adiponectin activation counteracts metabolic and mitochondrial disturbances that drive adverse remodeling after reperfusion.
abstract: Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived hormone with broad cardiometabolic benefits, circulating at high levels in healthy individuals but reduced in obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Low adiponectin concentrations are strongly associated with coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury (MIRI), and heart failure. MIRI remains a major unmet need in contemporary ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) care. Although reperfusion is essential in limiting ischemic myocardial necrosis, it causes deleterious effects such as impaired carbohydrate oxidation, excessive fatty-acid oxidation, intracellular acidosis, calcium (Ca 2+ ) overload, oxidative/nitrative stress, and mitochondrial fragmentation, that expand infarct size, worsen microvascular obstruction, and fuel adverse ventricular remodeling. Activation of the adiponectin-adiponectin receptor (AdipoR) axis directly counteracts these processes by stimulating adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent metabolic rebalancing, restoring mitochondrial fusion-fission homeostasis, enhancing oxidative capacity, reducing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS-) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase-mediated injury, improving endothelial nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability, and enhancing microvascular perfusion. In animal models, adiponectin or its mimetics consistently reduced infarct size, improved myocardial function, and attenuated apoptosis, inflammation, and no-reflow. A growing array of therapeutic strategies has emerged, each bringing its own pharmacologic nuances and implications for translation to the clinic. This review summarizes current strategies to enhance adiponectin action, highlights the progress in peptide and small-molecule mimetics, and discusses future directions for clinical translation in cardiometabolic diseases.
ids: title:prospects for adiponectin based therapeutics in myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury

title: Cardiomyocyte-enriched OTUD5 alleviates pathological myocardial hypertrophy by deubiquitinating STAT3 and modulating the STAT3-PGC-1α axis.
summary: Investigated the role of the deubiquitinase OTUD5 in pathological cardiac hypertrophy using cardiomyocyte‑specific knockout and overexpression in mouse models of angiotensin II infusion and transverse aortic constriction. Demonstrated that OTUD5 removes K63‑linked ubiquitin from STAT3, suppressing its phosphorylation and nuclear entry, thereby relieving repression of PGC‑1α and improving mitochondrial function. The OTUD5‑STAT3‑PGC‑1α axis links ubiquitin signaling to metabolic adaptation in hypertrophy.
abstract: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy presents a important public health challenge, particularly in aging populations, highlighting the urgent need for novel therapeutic targets. This study investigates the role and molecular mechanisms of OTUD5 in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. OTUD5 expression is greatly increased in cardiomyocytes from hypertrophic hearts. Deleting cardiomyocyte-specific OTUD5 exacerbates myocardial hypertrophy induced by angiotensin II (Ang II) and transverse aortic constriction (TAC). By contrast, targeted overexpression of OTUD5 in cardiomyocytes alleviates Ang II-induced pathological hypertrophy. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that OTUD5 regulates STAT3 activity by removing the K63-linked ubiquitin chain at lysine 283 (K283) on STAT3 through its C224 residue. This process inhibits both phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of STAT3, effectively relieving its transcriptional repression of PGC1α and enhancing mitochondrial function within cardiomyocytes. Our research uncovers a new OTUD5-STAT3-PGC1α axis that modulates mitochondrial bioenergetics, suggesting it as a potential therapeutic target for pathological cardiac hypertrophy.
ids: title:cardiomyocyte enriched otud5 alleviates pathological myocardial hypertrophy by deubiquitinating stat3 and modulating the stat3 pgc 1 axis

title: PKP2 orchestrates OXPHOS expression in cardiomyocytes via a PGC1α-dependent mechanism.
abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) is an inherited cardiac disease in which most patients carry (likely) pathogenic variants in desmosomal genes, most commonly in plakophilin-2 (PKP2). While the genetic causes are well described, the molecular mechanisms driving disease progression-particularly in response to exercise-remain poorly understood. To investigate disease-driving pathways in ACM, we used PKP2 mutant human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) and myocardial tissue from ACM patients. Transcriptomic profiling revealed consistent downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes in PKP2 mutant hiPSC-CMs, which was confirmed in explanted ACM hearts carrying PKP2 variants. Reduced expression of OXPHOS-related genes was associated with lower PPARGC1A expression and decreased mitochondrial spare capacity in PKP2 mutant hiPSC-CMs. The reduction in PPARGC1A expression appeared to result, at least in part, from decreased AMPKα protein levels, a known activator of PPARGC1A previously shown to localize at the intercalated disc, as PKP2 mutant cells failed to increase PPARGC1A expression following treatment with AICAR, an AMPK activator. To directly assess whether increasing PPARGC1A expression could compensate for this defect, we overexpressed PPARGC1A, which partially restored OXPHOS gene expression and improved contractility in PKP2 mutant cells. Our study identifies a novel transcriptional mechanism linking PKP2 loss to reduced mitochondrial function via decreased PGC1α signaling, partially through reduced AMPKα levels. Disruption of this axis reduces OXPHOS gene expression and mitochondrial function in PKP2 mutant hiPSC-CMs, potentially impairing the heart's ability to meet increased energy demands during stress, and offering a mechanistic explanation for the detrimental effects of exercise in ACM. Furthermore, these findings highlight PGC1α induction as a potential therapeutic strategy to restore OXPHOS gene expression and mitochondrial adaptability in ACM.
ids: title:pkp2 orchestrates oxphos expression in cardiomyocytes via a pgc1 dependent mechanism

title: Lysosomal protein transmembrane 5 protects against myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury by promoting mitophagy via the NEDD4-LC3 axis.
abstract: Background Mitophagy is essential for mitochondrial quality control during myocardial ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury. Lysosomal protein transmembrane 5 (LAPTM5) has been implicated in cardiovascular disease and autophagy, but its role in cardiac mitophagy remains unclear. Methods LAPTM5 knockout mice and cardiomyocyte-targeted AAV9-cTnT-LAPTM5 were used to determine the role of LAPTM5 in myocardial I/R injury. Cardiomyocyte hypoxia/reoxygenation models, mt-Keima imaging, mitochondrial fractionation, LC3-mitochondrial colocalization, co-immunoprecipitation, molecular docking, site-directed mutagenesis, NEDD4 gain- and loss-of-function, and p62 ubiquitination assays were used to investigate the underlying mechanism. Depending on data distribution and group number, appropriate parametric or non-parametric statistics were applied together with correction for multiple testing. Results LAPTM5 expression progressively decreased following I/R or H/R stress. LAPTM5 deficiency aggravated myocardial injury, cardiac dysfunction, and mitochondrial structural and functional damage, whereas LAPTM5 overexpression attenuated these abnormalities. LAPTM5 promoted mitophagy by enhancing LC3 recruitment to mitochondria. Mechanistically, LAPTM5 recruited NEDD4 to mitochondria through its PY3 motif and facilitated NEDD4-LC3 complex formation. NEDD4 depletion abolished LAPTM5-mediated mitophagy and cytoprotection, whereas re-expression of NEDD4-WT, but not the E3-inactive NEDD4-CS mutant, restored these effects. NEDD4-WT also increased p62 ubiquitination. AAV9-mediated LAPTM5 re-expression reduced infarct size, improved cardiac function, and preserved mitochondrial integrity in LAPTM5-deficient hearts. Conclusions LAPTM5 protects against myocardial I/R injury by promoting mitophagy through the NEDD4-LC3 axis. PY3-dependent recruitment of NEDD4 and its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity facilitate LC3-associated mitochondrial clearance, accompanied by enhanced p62 ubiquitination, thereby preserving mitochondrial homeostasis during reperfusion.
ids: title:lysosomal protein transmembrane 5 protects against myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury by promoting mitophagy via the nedd4 lc3 axis

title: Exposomic Determinants in Heart Failure Among Older Adults - Mechanistic Links, Clinical Evidence, and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Heart failure (HF) in older adults emerges from the interplay between biological aging and the totality of environmental and behavioural exposures conceptualized as the exposome. Traditional cardiovascular risk factors and intrinsic cardiac pathology only partially explain HF burden, as chronic exposures to air pollution, traffic noise, temperature extremes, toxic metals and chemicals, artificial light at night, and adverse social environments, along with low greenness and walkability, substantially influence HF incidence, decompensations, and prognosis in older patients with multiple comorbidities. Recently, epidemiological studies have associated many of the exposomic factors with HF incidence and morbidity. Age‑related impairments of the myocardium and vasculature make them particularly vulnerable to external stressors. Mechanistically, aging, HF, and environmental factors converge on shared pathways including, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammaging, impaired autophagy and proteostasis, genomic and epigenetic alterations, cellular senescence, dysregulated neurohormonal and circadian signalling, and fibrosis with maladaptive remodelling. Through these mechanisms exposome chronically accelerates cardiovascular aging and lowers the threshold for HF onset and progression. This review considers a shift from an organ‑centred view of HF in older adults to a systems‑level, life‑course perspective that explicitly incorporates exposomic determinants, and argues that reducing harmful exposures while promoting green space, physical activity, walkability, and healthy dietary patterns should be integral to HF prevention and management strategies in aging societies.
ids: title:exposomic determinants in heart failure among older adults mechanistic links clinical evidence and future perspectives

title: Clinical Reference Percentiles for AI-derived Epicardial Adipose Tissue: A Multicenter Study.
journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
abstract: Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) has emerged as an important cardiovascular biomarker that reflects both inflammatory and cardiometabolic risk. EAT volume and density vary significantly across populations, yet there is a lack of multicenter studies investigating the predictive value of population-specific EAT percentiles. In this multicenter study, we retrospectively analyzed low-dose computed tomography correction scans from 42,842 patients undergoing myocardial perfusion imaging. A derivation cohort of 15,082 patients was used to establish sex- and age-specific nomograms for EAT density and EAT volume indexed to body surface area. Percentile-based thresholds were tested for outcome prediction in a validation cohort of 27,760 patients. For clinical implementation, we developed an online EAT percentile calculator. Percentile curves demonstrated increased BSA-indexed EAT volume and decreasing EAT density with age. Over a median follow-up of 3.6 years (IQR: 1.83 - 5.14), 4,956 patients experienced a nonfatal myocardial infarction or death. In multivariable Cox models, patients above the 95th sex- and age-specific percentile had significantly worse outcomes for BSA-indexed EAT volume [adjusted hazard ratio 1.30, 95% CI: 1.14 - 1.49, p < 0.001] and EAT density [adjusted hazard ratio 1.7, 95% CI: 1.51 - 1.92, p<0.001] when compared to patients below the 50th percentile (p<0.001). Age- and sex-specific EAT percentiles provide a clinically interpretable framework for contextualizing automated EAT measurements and identifying patients at increased cardiovascular risk. EAT density was a stronger prognostic marker and identified elevated risk even among patients with normal BMI, supporting its potential to provide information beyond conventional anthropometric assessment.
ids: title:clinical reference percentiles for ai derived epicardial adipose tissue a multicenter study

title: A futile Na<sup>+</sup> K<sup>+</sup> transport cycle augments energy expenditure in beige adipocytes.
abstract: Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1)-independent energy dissipation has been proven to serve physiological functions in beige adipocytes. Here we show that a futile sodium/potassium (Na + /K + ) transport cycle is preferentially amplified in mouse and human beige adipocytes and contributes to UCP1-independent energy expenditure. In mice, cold exposure activates a sympathetic-thyroid hormone signaling axis that coordinatedly induces the Na + /K + -ATPase subunit ATP1A2 together with Na + and K + channels, increasing bidirectional ion flux across the plasma membrane while maintaining ionic balance. Atp1a2 + Kcnk3 + adipocytes are detected in mouse inguinal white adipose tissue after cold exposure. Acute inhibition of Na + /K + -ATPase reduces energy expenditure in mouse and human beige adipocytes, whereas overexpressing Atp1a2 in murine adipocytes potentiates energy expenditure, independent of UCP1. Adipocyte-specific Atp1a2 deletion impairs thermogenic capacity and exacerbates diet-induced obesity in mice. Expression of a human ATP1A2 missense variant reduces ATP1A2-dependent respiration in mouse adipocytes. Together, these identify ion transport as a tunable ATP-consuming mechanism that expands the thermogenic repertoire of beige adipocytes.
ids: title:a futile na sup sup k sup sup transport cycle augments energy expenditure in beige adipocytes

title: Specific effects of Pulsed Field Ablation on the cardiac tissue, the nervous system and the conduction system in experimental and clinical studies.
journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology
abstract: Aims Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a novel ablation modality for the treatment of cardiac arrhythmias and has rapidly reshaped contemporary electrophysiology practice. This article provides a comprehensive analysis on the mechanisms underlying the specific effects of PFA on myocardial, neural tissue structures, and the cardiac conduction system, integrating biophysical principles with preclinical and clinical evidence relevant to contemporary electrophysiology practice. Methods and results This document provides an exhaustive mechanistic explanation for the preferential effects of PFA on myocardium and the limits of the 'tissue-selectivity' concept. The complex interplay between cellular and tissue-level biophysics, biological responses, and tissue regenerative capacity that determines differential susceptibility to electroporation across tissues is analysed. Distinct patterns of lesion formation and maturation following PFA are also reviewed, highlighting the temporal and histopathological differences compared with radiofrequency ablation. Additionally, lesion formation in heterogeneous substrates is analysed, including fibrotic and adipose-rich myocardium, where local electric field distribution critically influences lesion durability. Conclusion The article further examines the interaction between pulsed electric fields and neural tissue, with emphasis on the phrenic nerve and intrinsic cardiac autonomic nervous system. While nerve stimulation and transient reversible conduction disturbances produced by reversible electroporation can occur during ablation, permanent neural injury appears extremely rare in current clinical experience. Finally, this manuscript examines current understanding regarding the specific effects of PFA on the cardiac conduction system, which according to the limited available evidence appear strongly dependent on electric field dose and anatomical proximity.
ids: 10.1093/europace/euag208
title:specific effects of pulsed field ablation on the cardiac tissue the nervous system and the conduction system in experimental and clinical studies

title: Bergenin attenuates diabetic cardiomyopathy by inhibiting oxidative stress and ferroptosis through modulation of the YAP signaling axis.
abstract: Aims Diabetes mellitus-associated cardiac dysfunction arises from metabolic imbalance, oxidative stress, inflammation, maladaptive remodeling, and impaired cardiac performance. Bergenin (BER), a naturally occurring small molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic regulatory properties, has shown therapeutic potential; however, its role in diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) remains unclear. This study investigated the cardioprotective effects of BER in DCM, with particular emphasis on oxidative stress, the Hippo-Yes-associated protein (YAP), and ferroptosis signaling axis. Materials and methods DCM was induced in rats using a high-fat diet combined with low-dose streptozotocin (STZ). Diabetic rats received BER (25 or 50 mg/kg/day) or empagliflozin (10 mg/kg/day). Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography, followed by histopathological and molecular analyses. To further investigate the underlying mechanisms, H9c2 cardiomyoblasts exposed to high glucose were used for in vitro assessment of oxidative stress, Hippo-YAP signaling, and ferroptosis-related markers. Key findings In vivo, BER treatment significantly improved cardiac function, attenuated histopathological injury, and reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and fibrosis in diabetic rats. Consistent with these findings, in vitro, BER reduced reactive oxygen species generation, restored mitochondrial integrity, and prevented high glucose-induced injury in H9c2 cells. Mechanistically, BER modulated YAP signaling and suppressed ferroptosis-related changes. YAP silencing attenuated the protective effects of BER, supporting a critical role for YAP in mediating its anti-ferroptotic effects. Significance These findings demonstrate that BER exerts cardioprotective effects against diabetes-associated cardiac dysfunction and provide mechanistic evidence implicating the YAP-ferroptosis axis in this protection. Further studies are warranted to establish its translational potential.
ids: title:bergenin attenuates diabetic cardiomyopathy by inhibiting oxidative stress and ferroptosis through modulation of the yap signaling axis

title: Atrial Cardiomyopathy Through the Pathologist's Lens: From Tissue Remodeling to Clinical Expression.
journal: Cardiovascular pathology : the official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology
abstract: Atrial cardiomyopathy (ACM) provides a useful framework for understanding structural, architectural, contractile, and electrophysiological disease of the atria. ACM and atrial fibrillation (AF) are closely linked but are not interchangeable: ACM favors arrhythmogenesis, whereas sustained AF can accelerate atrial injury. This review considers ACM from the pathologist's perspective, encompassing primary atrial disease and secondary remodeling associated with valvular disease and classical cardiomyopathies. The histologic spectrum includes cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and myocytolysis, interstitial and replacement fibrosis, endocardial fibroelastosis, adipose and inflammatory infiltration, vascular injury, and amyloid deposition. Structural remodeling is regionally heterogeneous, and appendage specimens may underrepresent abnormalities elsewhere in the atrium. Histologic interpretation requires attention to intrinsic regional architecture, associated lesions, previous interventions, and methods of quantification. At the molecular and cellular level, genetic susceptibility and acquired stressors converge on cardiomyocyte dysfunction, inflammation, fibroblast activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Correlating these tissue changes with mapping, imaging, biomarkers, and clinical outcomes will be necessary to validate noninvasive phenotypes and identify clinically meaningful disease subsets. At present, ACM should prompt etiologic investigation and risk assessment but does not by itself constitute an indication for specific therapy.
ids: title:atrial cardiomyopathy through the pathologist s lens from tissue remodeling to clinical expression
