title: Beyond Hemodynamics: Uremic Toxins, Post-Translational Modifications, and Inflammatory-Metabolic Remodeling in Uremic Cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Uremic cardiomyopathy has traditionally been attributed to pressure overload, volume overload, hypertension, and neurohormonal activation in chronic kidney disease. However, growing experimental and clinical evidence indicates that nonhemodynamic mechanisms also contribute to myocardial remodeling in uremia. These mechanisms include retention of uremic toxins and protein-bound solutes, mediators of mineral metabolism, gut-derived metabolites, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and post-translational protein modifications. In this review, we discuss uremic cardiomyopathy as a systemic inflammatory-metabolic disorder in which kidney failure reshapes myocardial structure and function through interacting biochemical and interorgan pathways. We first define the major classes of uremic toxins, including small water-soluble solutes, middle molecules, protein-bound uremic toxins, and reactive chemical intermediates. We then focus on post-translational modifications, particularly urea-derived cyanate-mediated carbamylation, a well-characterized uremia-associated mechanism that can alter collagen, extracellular matrix turnover, plasma proteins, lipoproteins, and potentially long-lived cardiac proteins. Additional injury pathways, including oxidative modifications, ferroptosis, fibroblast growth factor 23/Klotho imbalance, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation by indoxyl sulfate, gut-derived adrenergic metabolites, endotoxemia, and inflammasome signaling, are discussed as complementary and partially overlapping mechanisms. Because much of the current mechanistic evidence comes from preclinical models, circulating biomarkers, or associative human studies, we distinguish established evidence from plausible mechanistic hypotheses throughout the review. Finally, we discuss therapeutic implications, including enhanced toxin removal, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, and future strategies targeting uremic toxins, proteostasis, ferroptosis, inflammasome activation, and toxin-induced post-translational modifications.
ids: title:beyond hemodynamics uremic toxins post translational modifications and inflammatory metabolic remodeling in uremic cardiomyopathy

title: Co-administration of empagliflozin and curcumin attenuates the development of MASLD by modulating lipid metabolism and adipose tissue browning in HFD-fed C57BL/6J mice.
abstract: The increasing global incidence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) highlights the need for effective treatment strategies. This study investigated the combined effects of empagliflozin (EMPA), a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, and curcumin (Cur), a natural polyphenol, on MASLD development in mice. Male C57BL/6J mice were fed a normal chow diet (NCD) or a high-fat diet (HFD) for 23 weeks. HFD-fed mice received EMPA, Cur, or their combination throughout the dietary intervention. Markers of lipid metabolism, thermogenesis, and oxidative stress were evaluated. In vivo adipose tissue browning was assessed via 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging. Co-administration of EMPA and Cur significantly attenuated body weight gain (p < 0.001 vs. HFD) and adipose tissue expansion without altering food intake. Glucose tolerance and hepatic AKT phosphorylation were markedly improved (p < 0.001). Hepatic TG content and MASLD Activity Score were substantially reduced (p < 0.001), accompanied by AMPK activation, FAS suppression, and CPT1A upregulation. Fecal TG content was elevated with combination treatment (p < 0.001 vs. HFD), indicating reduced intestinal lipid absorption. BAT thermogenic activity, confirmed by 18F-FDG PET/CT and cold tolerance testing, and sWAT browning were most pronounced in the combination group. Hepatic oxidative stress markers were most improved by the combination, accompanied by Nrf2 pathway activation. Co-administration of EMPA and Cur represents a multi-target approach for mitigating MASLD development. This effect entails comprehensive improvement of metabolic homeostasis, reduced hepatic steatosis, and increased systemic energy expenditure. Formal combination interaction analysis indicated synergistic effects across key metabolic endpoints.
ids: title:co administration of empagliflozin and curcumin attenuates the development of masld by modulating lipid metabolism and adipose tissue browning in hfd fed c57bl 6j mice

title: MitoFLUX-EM reveals damaged mitochondria are captured by pre-existing mitolysosomes during PINK1-dependent mitophagy in the heart
abstract: Abstract Damaged mitochondria are cleared by PINK1-Parkin mitophagy, but the pathway is incompletely understood in vivo. Here, we developed MitoFLUX-EM, combining electron microscopy with nanoscale ¹⁵N isotope tracing to resolve the temporal sequence of mitophagy intermediates in vivo, and applied it to a cardiomyopathy mouse model (CHCHD10 S59L) with high PINK1-dependent mitophagy. Unexpectedly, we found that damaged mitochondria are directly captured by pre-existing mitolysosomes, resulting in multisegmented mitolysosomes that sequestered as many as 33 mitochondria at distinct stages of ultrastructural degradation. Autophagosomal-like membranes arising from the mitolysosomes preferentially engaged the intact outer membrane of damaged mitochondria and neither protein removal nor rupture of the outer membrane was required for mitophagy, contrary to prior models. Pink1 loss disrupted this pathway, causing accumulation of aggregates within mitochondria and reduced survival. These findings reveal that PINK1-dependent mitophagy proceeds through a novel form of microautophagy to safeguard cardiac mitochondrial quality in vivo and establish MitoFLUX-EM as a platform for resolving organelle turnover.
ids: title:mitoflux em reveals damaged mitochondria are captured by pre existing mitolysosomes during pink1 dependent mitophagy in the heart

title: Platelet-macrophage crosstalk in cardiac inflammation and remodeling.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular cell research
abstract: Cardiac injury and chronic heart disease are increasingly recognized as multicellular processes driven by dynamic interactions between immune and thrombotic signaling networks. Although platelets and macrophages have been extensively studied individually, the molecular mechanisms through which their reciprocal interactions regulate cardiac inflammation and remodeling remain incompletely defined. A comprehensive understanding of this cellular crosstalk is needed to define the signaling pathways that couple acute injury responses to chronic maladaptive remodeling. Among these interactions, platelet-macrophage crosstalk has emerged as an important regulator of inflammatory responses and tissue remodeling within the injured myocardium. Beyond their traditional roles in hemostasis and innate immunity, platelets communicate with macrophages through adhesion molecules, soluble mediators, and extracellular vesicles, thereby modulating macrophage activation and functional reprogramming. Platelet-derived mediators, including P-selectin, CD40L, PF4 (CXCL4), CCL5, and platelet-derived extracellular vesicles, modulate macrophage inflammatory signaling, cytokine production, redox balance, metabolic reprogramming, and pro-fibrotic responses relevant to cardiac remodeling. During acute myocardial injury, these interactions facilitate immune-cell recruitment, efferocytosis, and tissue repair, whereas persistent platelet-macrophage communication promotes chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and progression to heart failure. This review summarizes current molecular insights into platelet-macrophage interactions, focusing on receptor-mediated signaling, extracellular vesicle cargo transfer, immunometabolic regulation, and redox-dependent pathways. We also discuss emerging evidence linking this axis to trained immunity and inflammatory memory and highlight potential molecular targets for modulating maladaptive immune remodeling in cardiovascular disease.
ids: title:platelet macrophage crosstalk in cardiac inflammation and remodeling

title: Macrophage-Derived Glycoprotein Nonmetastatic Melanoma Protein B Attenuates Cardiac Dysfunction by Promoting Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-Independent Angiogenesis.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: Background Pressure overload-induced heart failure involves maladaptive cardiac remodeling and inadequate angiogenesis. The limitations of VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor)-based therapies underscore the need to identify alternative angiogenic pathways. GPNMB (glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B) is a macrophage-secreted protein implicated in tissue repair, but its role in pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling and its potential to modulate angiogenesis remain unknown. Methods Myeloid-specific Gpnmb knockout and control mice were subjected to transverse aortic constriction. Cardiac function, remodeling, and capillary density were assessed. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed to identify transcriptomic changes. In vitro, human endothelial cells were treated with recombinant GPNMB to assess proliferation, migration, and tube formation, and to dissect the underlying signaling pathways. The therapeutic potential of Gpnmb overexpression was evaluated using AAV9 vectors. Results Myeloid Gpnmb deletion exacerbated transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy, fibrosis, and capillary rarefaction. Single-cell sequencing revealed a reduced capillary endothelial cell population and pathway enrichment indicative of endothelial dysfunction and metabolic reprogramming in myeloid-specific Gpnmb knockout hearts. Mechanistically, GPNMB directly promoted endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and tube formation by activating the mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) pathway in a CD44-dependent manner, independently of VEGF signaling. Cardiac-specific Gpnmb overexpression rescued angiogenesis, improved cardiac function, and attenuated pathological remodeling after transverse aortic constriction. Conclusions Macrophage-derived GPNMB is a critical regulator of cardiac adaptation to pressure overload. It promotes a VEGF-independent angiogenic program probably via the CD44/mTOR axis, as supported by in vitro mechanistic studies. GPNMB represents a promising therapeutic target for heart failure characterized by microvascular rarefaction.
ids: title:macrophage derived glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein b attenuates cardiac dysfunction by promoting vascular endothelial growth factor independent angiogenesis

title: Dual inhibition of SGLT 1 and 2 by sotagliflozin alleviates intracellular sodium overload and improves cardiometabolic remodelling in uraemic cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Aims Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is associated with uraemic cardiomyopathy characterized by early metabolic dysfunction. Elevated myocardial intracellular sodium (Naᵢ) has emerged as a driver of cardiometabolic remodelling, however, its role in CKD and therapeutic modulation remains unclear. We investigated whether dual sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT)1/2 inhibition with sotagliflozin (SOTA) targets Naᵢ and improves cardiac metabolism in CKD. Methods and results CKD was induced in male Wistar rats by 5/6 nephrectomy and assessed after 4 weeks. Cardiac phenotype was evaluated using in vivo echocardiography and ex vivo Langendorff perfusion combined with 23Na and 31P NMR spectroscopy. CKD hearts exhibited preserved systolic but impaired diastolic function and a marked elevation in myocardial Naᵢ, identifying Naᵢ overload as an early feature of uraemic cardiomyopathy. Cardiac metabolomic profiling and flux modelling demonstrated widespread suppression of central carbon metabolism, redox imbalance despite preserved PCr/ATP. In silico electrophysiological simulations predicted Naᵢ-driven Ca2+ dysregulation consistent with in vivo diastolic dysfunction. Chronic SOTA treatment (3 weeks, in vivo) normalized myocardial Naᵢ and partially reversed metabolic remodelling. Acute SOTA exposure (20 min, Langendorff-perfusion) similarly reduced Naᵢ in CKD hearts but not in controls, indicating a direct, disease-selective myocardial effect. Naᵢ normalization was accompanied by improved redox state and restoration of mitochondrial metabolic flux, without changes in expression of canonical Na + -handling proteins. Conclusion Myocardial Naᵢ overload emerges as an early and potentially modifiable feature of uraemic cardiomyopathy. Dual SGLT1/2 inhibition with SOTA directly lowers Naᵢ and improves cardiac metabolic homeostasis, supporting Naᵢ as a mechanistically relevant and potentially targetable pathway in CKD-related cardiac remodelling.
ids: title:dual inhibition of sglt 1 and 2 by sotagliflozin alleviates intracellular sodium overload and improves cardiometabolic remodelling in uraemic cardiomyopathy

title: Circadian mechanisms in heart failure: Cell-specific regulation and chrono-medicine.
abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that circadian rhythms profoundly influence the pathophysiology of heart failure (HF). The circadian clock system governs myocardial functions via synchronized actions from multiple cell types involving cardiomyocytes and non-cardiomyocytes. This review summarizes state-of-the-art advances on the cardiovascular circadian system and provides a perspective on time-of-day effects in the pathophysiology of HF, including energy metabolism, tissue inflammation and fibrosis. In particular, we focus on cell-specific circadian regulation and synthesize how circadian clocks across cardiomyocytes, vascular cells, fibroblasts, and adipocytes interact to regulate the pathophysiology of HF. Based on this framework, we discuss how synchronizing internal and external time cues via clock-modulating compounds and/or time-restricted eating (TRE) may prevent HF or facilitate rehabilitation. Together, this Review provides a timely synthesis of current understanding of HF as a function of biological timing and highlights potential chronotherapeutic strategies.
ids: title:circadian mechanisms in heart failure cell specific regulation and chrono medicine

title: Cardiovascular effects of metyrapone treatment in patients with mild autonomous cortisol secretion: a secondary analysis.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
abstract: Context Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) is associated with increased mortality, mainly because of cardiovascular disease. Objective Here we investigated the effects of cortisol-lowering medical treatment on blood pressure regulation, cardiac fat depots, heart function and morphology, and other cardiovascular risk factors. Methods In this secondary analysis of our prospective, open-label, single-center study at the Medical University of Vienna, we investigated 15 patients with MACS (12 women; age 59 [53-64] years) before and after 12 weeks of treatment with evening doses of metyrapone (500 mg at 6 Pm and 250 mg at 10 Pm). Cardiac fat stores, morphology, and myocardial function were evaluated using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy. Orthostatic blood pressure regulation was measured by standardized protocols. Lipidomics, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system activity and branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) concentrations were assessed. Results Mean supine systolic (137 [121-139] vs 122 [115-129] mmHg; P = 0.041) and diastolic (89 [80-93] vs 75 [71-86] mmHg; P = .045) blood pressure decreased after treatment in patients without changes in concomitant antihypertensive medication. Epicardial fat was lower at follow-up compared to baseline (1032.70 [894.23-1482.90] vs 929.37 [736.12-1317.15] mm2; P = .022). No changes in paracardial and intramyocardial fat, as well as in cardiac function and morphology were observed. The aldosterone-to-angiotensin II ratio was lower at follow-up (1.56 [0.87-2.82] vs 1.21 [0.98-1.92]; P = .042) and alterations in lipid profiles, but not in BCAA levels, were identified. Conclusion Treatment with evening doses of metyrapone improved blood pressure and reduced epicardial adipose tissue.
ids: 10.1210/clinem/dgag228
title:cardiovascular effects of metyrapone treatment in patients with mild autonomous cortisol secretion a secondary analysis
